body:
Thanks for the issue! We get a lot of issues, so this message is automatically posted to each one to help you check that you've included all of the information we need to help you.

Reporting a bug? Please be sure to include:
1. The version of ESLint you are using (run `eslint -v`)
2. The source code that caused the problem
3. The configuration you're using (for the rule or your entire config file)
4. The actual ESLint output complete with line numbers

Requesting a new rule? Please be sure to include:
1. The use case for the rule - what is it trying to prevent or flag?
2. Whether the rule is trying to prevent an error or is purely stylistic
3. Why you believe this rule is generic enough to be included

Requesting a feature? Please be sure to include:
1. The problem you want to solve (don't mention the solution)
2. Your take on the correct solution to problem

Including this information in your issue helps us to triage it and get you a response as quickly as possible.

Thanks!

Okay, I think now I am entirely wrong about this being an issue with `no-undef` and "browser".  I realize now that `Document` is indeed a browser environment "global" that should not be redefined (distinct from `document`/`window.document`).

I think instead, this is an issue with the "commonjs" environment, and perhaps an issue with how environments are configured/applied when using the hierarchical inherited `.eslintrc` configuration.

I think that the expected behavior when adding the "commonjs" environment from the CLI w/o `.eslintrc` is correct, but via webpack w/ `.eslintrc` is not.  Adding a `/* eslint-env commonjs */` to the top of the file with issues makes the webpack case happy.

It's seems simply like the `{"env": {"browser": true, "commonjs": true}}` override for the file isn't picking up the CommonJS environment.

I'm not sure how to proceed; please advise!  Apologies for the noise, tracking this one down has been a learning experience.
I can reproduce this in online demo with `browser` environment vs. `browser + node` environment... This is pretty strange.
I will try to fix this.

Hmm, I remembered #3390.
In environments which have an extra scope (commonjs, node, and modules), this might be an intended behavior.

@mysticatea I think the error should go away when we add the "commonjs" environment, yes.  I apologize, but I think my second posting has the real issue.

I think the real issue is that the `.eslintrc` setup (per-dir w/ extra / changing envs), doesn't pick up on that properly for some reason.  I can try to create a repo that reproduces this, but it will be a minute before I can do that.

## 

Oh wow... that's strange that that issue deals with no-undef and case as well...  Is it possible that `Window` is actually a type in the "browser" environment, in addition to the `window` object?  That's what tripped me up in my initial post: `Document` is the name of type (and `document` is an instance of it); same for `Window`: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window, I think.

`Window` and `Document` are built-in global variables (those type is `function`).
`window` is an object which has `Window.prototype` as its `__proto__` value.

Though I'm not sure why the current `no-undef` behavior reports redeclarations....
Pretty sure that's due to the historical reasons. `no-undef` was one of the first rules. We didn't have `no-redeclare` at that point yet. But maybe we should revisit this now?

@ilyavolodin Thank you for the explanation.
I guess it needs difficult arrangement, so I would like to open new issue before 2.0.

@mysticatea :+1: 
Back to the original issue. So now with @mysticatea explanation I understand why `browser` + `commonjs` environments are not complaining about redeclaration of `Document`, but I still don't think that's correct. Both environments suggest that you will run code in both places (not necessarily at the same time), so when you are running it in browser, you should not be redeclaring `Document`, even if under commonjs that might be a reasonable thing to do. I have no idea how we implement this, since commonjs creates an extra top level scope.

Creating a `var Document = {}` in the browser + CommonJS environments should cause a `no-shadow` issue, not a "overwriting a read-only global" issue.  I think that's perfectly acceptable; if you shadow a global, that's your (CommonJS module's) problem.

@ilyavolodin said:

> Both environments suggest that you will run code in both places (not necessarily at the same time),

I disagree with this statement.  What you'd really want in that case (the "not necessarily at the same time" case) is to run the linter twice, for both environments separately.  If you somehow have code that needs to work in all three permutations, well... three linter runs.

Actually `no-redeclare` and `no-shadow` are handling the extra scope as global.

``` js
/* eslint-env commonjs */
/* eslint no-redeclare:[2,{builtinGlobals:true}], no-shadow:[2,{builtinGlobals:true}] */
var Object = 0;
```

```
test.js
  3:5  error  Object is already defined  no-redeclare

✖ 1 problem (1 error, 0 warnings)
```

But also I understand the request in #3390...
Built-in globals includes many general names, especially in browsers.
So if somebody are 100% sure extra scope is made, they expect to not handle it as redeclaration.

(Ah, this is "difficult arrangement" I said before)
I'm not sure there's a bug here. Can someone clarify?
